title: Houses and growers
subtitle: Who makes Champagne
objectives: Explain the role of the houses

steps.title: The houses
steps.body: Large houses, or maisons, like Moët & Chandon, Veuve Clicquot, Bollinger and Krug, own some vineyards but buy most grapes from about 16,000 growers. They blend across villages and years for a consistent house style, especially in non-vintage. Houses make about two-thirds of Champagne's sales.

steps.title: Growers
steps.body: Growers who make and sell their own Champagne are called récoltant-manipulants, labelled RM. Since the 1990s, grower Champagne has become popular for showing a single village or vineyard. Co-operatives, CM, pool members' grapes. Label codes tell you who made the wine.
steps.highlight: RM grower; NM house; CM co-op

steps.prompt: Match each label code to its meaning.
steps.explanation: The small code on the label reveals the producer type.

steps.title: The échelle des crus
steps.body: Champagne's villages were once ranked on a scale, the échelle des crus, which set grape prices: 17 villages were Grand Cru, 100%, and 42 Premier Cru, 90 to 99%. The price system ended in 2010, but the names still appear on labels.

steps.prompt: Most Champagne is sold by large houses that buy grapes.
steps.explanation: Yes. Houses account for about two-thirds of sales.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Houses blend grapes from many growers for a house style
Grower Champagne, RM, shows single villages
